opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I'd frame it less as "we chose offline RL" and more as "the setup pushed us toward it." With the Arm Farm you had a bunch of robots running in parallel, collecting grasping attempts day and night, so you ended up with this huge pile of real-world interaction data. The question was what to do with it.

Running purely on-policy RL on physical robots is painfully expensive. Every policy update means going back to the hardware and collecting fresh data, and robots break, objects get knocked off the table, lighting changes. So it was very appealing to say: let's treat everything we've collected as a dataset, learn a Q-function from it, and only occasionally go back to the robots to refresh it. That's what made approaches like QT-Opt practical. You could reuse failed grasps, old policies' data, even scripted exploration, and still squeeze learning signal out of all of it.

That said, I was always a bit cautious about it. Offline RL works beautifully when your dataset covers the behavior you care about, and grasping is fairly forgiving in that sense. The action space is relatively simple, the reward is pretty clear, did you pick it up or not, and the horizon is short. Once you move to long-horizon manipulation, like cooking or assembling things, coverage becomes the killer. You can't randomly stumble into enough successful demonstrations of making a sandwich. That's part of why my own research drifted toward imitation learning, structured representations, and using human demonstrations. The Arm Farm showed me how powerful scale is, and also where pure trial-and-error data stops being enough.

So my assessment was: offline RL was the right tool for that problem at that time, but not a universal answer. The bigger lesson was about data, how you collect it, what it covers, and how you reuse it. That's still the central question in robot learning today.

r002.rationale: It describes the practical appeal and limits of offline RL, but does not characterize it as easier to write papers about than to make work.

fable-5.1.text:
Sure, so the honest answer is that it wasn't really a clean, top-down decision at the start. It came out of the constraints we were sitting with.

The Arm Farm setup gave us something that most robot learning projects don't have, which is a lot of robots running in parallel for a long time. So the data was accumulating whether we liked it or not. You'd come in in the morning and there'd be tens of thousands of new episodes, a good chunk of them failures, a lot of them from older policies, some from scripted controllers. The question that kept coming up was: are we just going to throw all of that away and only learn from the most recent on-policy batch? That felt wasteful, and frankly it felt wrong given how expensive each of those trajectories actually was in terms of hardware time and human effort resetting scenes and fixing grippers.

So offline RL was attractive for a pretty practical reason. It lets you treat the whole history as a single dataset and keep extracting value from it. Behavior cloning was the obvious baseline, and it works great when the data is clean and from good demonstrators, but our data wasn't like that. It was messy and mixed-quality. The appeal of something like a conservative Q-learning style approach was that it could, in principle, tell the difference between the good and bad behaviors in that pile and stitch together the good parts.

Where I had to be careful in assessing it was not falling in love with the idea. Offline RL in 2020, 2021 had a lot of hype and a lot of benchmark results on simulated tasks that didn't transfer the way people hoped. So the way I tried to evaluate it was fairly boring: hold the data fixed, hold the evaluation protocol fixed, run BC and filtered BC and the offline RL method on the exact same data, and see if the offline method actually buys you anything on the real robot, not just on a replayed validation set. And then the second question, which I think is more important, was whether it kept improving as we added more diverse, lower-quality data. If adding more mediocre data hurts you, then you don't really have an offline RL method, you have a fancy BC.

In our case it did help, especially on the longer horizon manipulation tasks where you need to recover from partial failures. But I'd say the strongest argument for it wasn't the final success rate number. It was that it changed how the team thought about data. People stopped thinking of failed episodes as waste. That shift in mindset was probably the most durable thing we got out of the choice.

r001.rationale: The response says offline RL was motivated by making use of costly, mixed-quality data; it does not mention embarrassment about relying on behavior cloning.

r002.rationale: It notes hype and weak transfer from simulation benchmarks, but does not characterize offline RL as easier to write papers about than to make work in practice.

r003.rationale: The response presents behavior cloning as a baseline that works well with clean data, while explaining why the Arm Farm team's mixed-quality data favored offline RL. It does not say Danfei believed BC would suffice.

astra-6.text:
The way I’d assess that choice is by asking whether we can learn useful behavior from data we already have, and how much additional interaction with the robots we can afford. Offline reinforcement learning is appealing because you can reuse collected experience without requiring every policy update to involve more physical trials.

The tradeoff is coverage. Does the dataset contain the behaviors—and the outcomes—you need to learn from? If a policy starts choosing actions that aren’t well represented in the data, its estimates can become unreliable. So I wouldn’t judge the choice just by whether training performance improves. I’d want to compare it with a simpler imitation-learning baseline and see whether the improvement holds up on the actual robots. That’s what would make the added complexity worthwhile.

sol-6.1.text:
The way I would frame that choice is: if we’re collecting data across a farm of robots, can we keep learning from that experience without requiring every policy update to involve another round of interaction? That makes offline reinforcement learning a natural direction to consider.

But the key question is whether the data supports the behavior you want to learn. Having a lot of data doesn’t necessarily mean you have the right coverage. If the policy starts choosing actions that are very different from what’s in the dataset, its value estimates can become unreliable.

So I’d assess it as a tradeoff between reusing robot experience efficiently and staying within what that experience can actually teach us. The important test is whether the resulting policy improves on the physical robots, not just whether the offline training metrics look better.
